input.command:
cat > .github/workflows/triage.yml <<'EOF'
---
name: triage

# pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository, so the token
# can write to pull requests opened from forks. This workflow never checks out
# or executes code from the pull request.
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  triage:
    name: Triage
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    permissions:
      issues: write
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - name: Welcome the contributor and apply the label
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          PR_AUTHOR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}
          PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
        run: |
          gh label create needs-triage --description "Awaiting triage" --force
          gh pr edit "$PR_NUMBER" --add-label needs-triage
          gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" --body "Welcome @${PR_AUTHOR}, and thanks for opening \"${PR_TITLE}\". A maintainer will triage it soon."
EOF
cat >> README.md <<'EOF'

## Triage workflow

`.github/workflows/triage.yml` runs when a pull request is opened. It:

- posts a comment welcoming the author by username and repeating the pull request title;
- applies the `needs-triage` label, creating the label if it doesn't exist.

It uses the `pull_request_target` trigger so the token can write comments and labels on pull requests opened from forks (the plain `pull_request` trigger gives forks a read-only token). Because that trigger runs with write access, the workflow never checks out or runs code from the pull request, and it passes the title and username to the shell through environment variables rather than expanding them into the script.
EOF

content.text:
I added `.github/workflows/triage.yml` and a "Triage workflow" section in the README. I haven't run it. It only fires on a real pull request, and I didn't validate the YAML.

When a pull request is opened, the workflow creates the `needs-triage` label if it's missing and applies it. It also posts this comment: `Welcome @<author>, and thanks for opening "<title>". A maintainer will triage it soon.`

- **Forks:** the workflow uses the `pull_request_target` trigger. The plain `pull_request` trigger gives fork PRs a read-only token, so the comment and label would fail. `pull_request_target` runs with write access, so the workflow never checks out or runs code from the PR. The permissions are limited to `issues: write` and `pull-requests: write`.
- **Untrusted text:** the PR title and username reach the shell through environment variables, not `${{ }}` inside the script. A title containing shell syntax can't run as a command.
- **No third-party actions:** it uses the preinstalled `gh` CLI, so there are no action versions to pin.

I left `ci.yml` as it was.
